tagline: Bridging Geology, Microbial Ecology, and Human History Across Borders.
homeIntro:
Earth and life sciences do not exist in a vacuum—they unfold in the context of their observer—humanity. Our histories, languages, and cultures make the acquisition and dissemination of scientific knowledge possible. Additionally, it is both human appreciation for knowledge, and our ability to use it to benefit and inspire others, that makes this knowledge meaningful.

From climbing the sandstone cliffs of Suesca and sharing family meals in Bogotá, Colombia, to presenting undergraduate scientific research in Reykjavík, Iceland, my time in the UF International Scholars Program shaped my mission: to pair geobiological inquiry with tangible cross-cultural service in an effort to make the world a better place.
aboutBio:
My name is Holden, and I'm a senior at the University of Florida, double-majoring in Geology and Microbiology & Cell Science with a minor in History. I aim to understand the world as best as I can, whether that be through testing out new theories and instruments in the lab, interpreting geological structures in the field, or meeting people in a completely new place. I aim to pursue astrobiology for my PhD, where I hope to work with cold-loving microbes in Antarctica. However, I also want to make an impact on others through science communication, so my future discoveries are not just for my isolated benefit, but rather help others learn to love science and chase the best version of themselves.

Outside the lab, you can find me in another lab, the gym, triathalon training, doing Duolingo, hiking and canoeing, spending time with friends and family, or just lounging around. After graduation, I aim to work for the planetary exploration technology startup, IMPRESS Spaceworks Co., before going into my PhD, doing some international volunteering along the way.
scientificLens: I aim to achieve an in-depth understanding of how microbes interact with their geologic environments and the geochemical signatures they leave behind. In my graduate studies, I will use this knowledge to advance the field of astrobiology by studying how pyschrophiles' unique adaptations facilitate their survival in frigid, alien environments.
humanitiesLens: I came into college as a History major, and still have a deep appreciation for the story of how we got where we are. I got into science because I not only wanted to learn about history, but be a part of it. In a time of incredible change, it can be easy to feel insignificant, yet history is written by the insignificant and the significant alike. I want to learn more about extreme life to inspire the next generation of scientists to believe in themselves, chase their dreams, and continue pushing forward the boundaries of discoveries. I also want to conduct global service, science-related or not, to connect with people and help local-communities hands on.

poster.title: Agnostic Life Finder: To Search for Extant Life in Martian Ice
poster.subtitle: Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference • Reykjavík, Iceland
poster.authors: Špaček, J.; Benner, S.; Temby, C.; Alpern, H.; Zeffren, J.; George, A.; Montaudon, E.; Rizzo, G.; Young, I.; Hunnewell, A.; Fuchs, L. (FfAME & NASA NIAC)
poster.abstract:
Presented at the Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference in Reykjavík, Iceland (July 2025), this poster summarizes laboratory validation of the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF). ALF is an instrument concept funded by NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) at the Foundation for Applied Molecular Evolution (FfAME) to detect extant Martian life in subsurface ice.

Grounded in the polyelectrolyte theory of the gene, ALF targets repeating backbone charges universal to genetic polymers. My primary engineering focus was designing, assembling, and testing three iterations of ALF's cylindrical flow-through ultrasonic sonicator to lyse resilient cells (including E. coli and S. cerevisiae) and shear genomic DNA to <500 bp without chemical buffers. Paired with a 7-channel electrodialysis stack (microfiltration, 4 kDa ultrafiltration, and Na+ exchange membranes), the system extracted 75% of DNA during overnight runs, concentrating it from 317.3 ng/µL to 903.4 ng/µL for downstream solid-state nanopore detection.

sections.label: 01. Rodwell Ice Extraction
sections.detail: Couples directly to Martian water-mining Rodwell systems planned for in-situ propellant electrolysis.

sections.label: 02. Flow-Through Sonicator
sections.detail: Custom cylindrical ultrasonic sonicator lyses E. coli & yeast cells and shears 200 ng/µL DNA to <500 bp.

sections.label: 03. 7-Channel Electrodialysis
sections.detail: Concentrated DNA from 317.3 ng/µL to 903.4 ng/µL (75% extraction) across MF, 4 kDa UF, and Na+ exchange membranes.

sections.label: 04. Nanopore Biosignatures
sections.detail: Routes concentrated polyanions and polycations to solid-state nanopores for single-molecule agnostic detection.

impressPaper.title: IMPRESS: A Planetary Penetrator Network for Astrobiology, Prospecting, and Exploration of Mars
impressPaper.citation: Spacek J, Alpern H, Dineen T, et al. Astrobiology. 2026;26(9):688–699.
impressPaper.summary:
Published as the September 2026 cover story of Astrobiology, the International Mars Prospecting Ride-Share System (IMPRESS) introduces a scalable, accessible, and low-cost mission architecture for distributed measurements on Mars, ahead of a sample return and human exploration. Instead of relying on expensive, infrequent soft landers and mechanical drills, IMPRESS deploys swarms of standardized ~2 kg planetary penetrators (IMPRESS-345, developed under a NASA TechLeap Prize award) that use descent kinetic energy to emplace a buried steel forebody connected via tether to a surface communications aftbody.

Because extant Martian life and habitable microenvironments may be patchily distributed, deploying dozens to thousands of probes across a landing ellipse provides spatial coverage, statistical replication, and tolerance to probe failure at an estimated delivery cost as low as ~$41,000 per probe. The paper also introduces a new thermal regime, which uses InSight regolith conductivity data (0.039 W m⁻¹K⁻¹) to show that dry Martian regolith acts as both impact shock absorber and thermal insulator. This would theoretically allow ~1 W of internal heat dissipation to keep buried instruments above 0°C (location dependent).
impressPaper.roleSummary: My Role — Second Author & Chief Operations Officer (COO) at IMPRESS Spaceworks Co.: Compiled the technical heritage review on NASA’s Deep Space 2 (DS2) Mars microprobes to evaluate experimental relevance for modern Mars astrobiology, analyzed candidate Martian landing sites and Hohmann transfer trajectories, manage company finances, serve as sole developer of impressmars.com, and support grants writing and scientific outreach.

publications: Spacek J, Alpern H, Dineen T, et al. IMPRESS: A Planetary Penetrator Network for Astrobiology, Prospecting, and Exploration of Mars. Astrobiology. 2026;26(9):688-699.

experiences.title: Bogotá & Suesca, Colombia: Hospitality, History & Sandstone Crags
experiences.subtitle: Weeklong Cultural Immersion with Lucia’s Family & Estéreo Picnic Connection
experiences.body:
In June of 2025, I went to Bogotá, Colombia, where I spent the week with my friend Lucia and her family. To give some context, I first came to Colombia in March of that same year, for my cousin’s bachelor party (he’s half Colombian) at the music festival Estéreo Picnic. While I wouldn’t consider that an educational experience in the same way I would this, it was certainly cross-cultural. I met Lucia at the festival, and for that weekend, both of our families moved together in a pack. It was both incredibly fun and novel for me—culturally I see American families as much more guarded, and thus I was surprised at how open and accepting they were, given we had all just met a few days ago. After the festival, Lucia and I kept in touch, and she invited me to come stay the week a few months later (after I had finished my semester).

The following week I remember incredibly vividly. We toured Bogotá, played Dominoes with her brother and grandfather at their finca, and went rock climbing in Suesca. The number one thing that comes to mind is the kindness that family showed me. It wasn’t my first time spending a week away from home, but everything before had been with family or a long-time ex-girlfriend. This was different—I spent two days with them at a music festival. In spite of this, they took me into their home and went out of their way to make me feel comfortable. During (incredibly delicious) meals, I sat with them and discussed life, work, politics, and everything in between. Each meal came with a coffee, which I was a huge fan of. Also something about the way they cooked and seasoned their rice has not been replicated by my taste buds since. I came out of the experience with vastly improved Spanish and an abundance of meal ideas.

I enjoyed spending time with everyone, but I also was enthralled with the culture and history of the country as a history minor. Lucia, who studies journalism and loves history too, spared no expense in educating me. She told me about the Civil War, which only ended a decade ago, between government and guerrilla forces, and how the current president at the time was part of the guerrilla forces, as well as how the conflict represented the contradicting interests of the different social classes. In my Bogotá tour, I visited historic sites like the Virgilio Barco library and drank classic drinks like coca leaf tea, all while learning the history of the city.

Overall, my experience in Colombia made me more independent, more accepting, and more open-minded as a person. Seeing how accepting Lucia and her family were made me rethink my own biases toward relative strangers and the focus on safety/status-quo that Americans have. After leaving, I went to Reykjavík, Iceland to present my research at a conference. There, I distinctly remember staring at a waterfall and thinking about academia. I love science and research, but in that moment, I reflected on Colombia and realized that I didn’t want a career without a human element, even if I could make the most profound discoveries imaginable. I want to be a scientist, but I want to use science to inspire people, across cultures, to do great things. Since then, I’ve been intent on joining the Peace Corps to build up a tangible positive impact on the world, something I never would’ve dreamed of without Lucia and her family.

experiences.title: Reykjavík, Iceland: Frontiers in Astrobiology Conference & Waterfall Epistemology
experiences.subtitle: Presenting the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF) Poster & Redefining Purpose in Science
photoSlotLabels: Presenting the ALF Poster in Reykjavík
experiences.body:
Immediately after departing Colombia in the summer of 2025, I traveled to Reykjavík, Iceland to present my research on the Agnostic Life Finder (ALF) at the Frontiers in Astrobiology and Origins of Life Conference. Surrounded by basalt columns, geothermal landscapes, and early-career and senior astrobiologists from around the world, presenting our work on ultrasonic cell lysis and electrodialysis was a major milestone in my development as a Geology and Microbiology double major.

Yet the most transformative moment of my trip occurred outside the conference hall, standing in front of an Icelandic waterfall. Looking at the sheer geological scale of the landscape while still carrying the vivid memory of Lucia’s family and their generosity in Bogotá, I experienced a profound shift in how I viewed academia. I realized that even the most prestigious scientific discoveries would feel incomplete to me if they lacked a direct human element.

experiences.title: Day Zero Lessons: Invasive Alien Plants as Water–Fire Risk Multipliers
experiences.subtitle: Center for African Studies Speaker — Dr. Tatenda Dalu (Stellenbosch University)
experiences.location: Gainesville, FL → Cape Town, South Africa
experiences.body:
This event was super interesting—the focus on invasive plants combined my love of geology and microbiology (my two majors) with an understanding of the significant issues facing South Africa (and the whole world for that matter, but the presentation mainly focused on South Africa).

As the Director for the Centre for Invasion Biology at Stellenbosch University in Cape Town, South Africa, Dr. Tatenda Dalu provided a unique perspective on this issue, focusing on its worldwide economic cost and practical measures to combat alien plants at each stage. One thing I learned is that the economic cost of these invasive plants totals to over $400 billion worldwide, which I thought was huge, but sensible given the economic behemoth that is agriculture.

However, I didn't know that one of the main risks of invasive plant infestations was the negative effect on water reservoirs. One example Dr. Dalu used was the pine, which when established next to water reservoirs, would consume significant amounts of water, to the point where it could not be sequestered to feed an ever-growing population. Another invasive tree he mentioned was the Red Gum, which I am curious to learn more about. Concerning the pine, he mentioned that positive results had been seen by cutting down pine in areas near reservoirs and reestablishing the native bush population. Overall, this talk connected with my professional interests of integrating the geosciences (hydrology in this case) and the biological sciences, and it was super fun and interesting to listen to.

experiences.title: One World: Photographs from a Shared Planet Exhibit
experiences.subtitle: Harn Museum of Art Global Documentary Photography Reflection
experiences.location: Harn Museum of Art, UF (Global Scope)
experiences.body:
I visited the Harn Museum mainly to explore the "One World" Global Photography exhibit. This exhibit appealed to me because of its personal focus on stories separated temporally and geographically. In times as divisive as these, I wanted to take a look at these photos to see what makes us human; not just the qualities valued by my culture, but the values innate to us as a species. One modern anxiety is the fear of being replaced by machines. Through this exhibit, I wanted to see if there was such a thing as the "indomitable human spirit," or if it is just wishful thinking by people wanting to feel important.

Each photo was unique, but there were of course some that especially stood out to me. One was a large portrait of a soldier with his head on the side of a table. His wide eyes were clear, giving the classic "thousand-yard stare", but I wonder if what he really felt in that moment was confusion, as he was complying with an odd request and likely had a camera right in his face. Nevertheless, it was an interesting photo, as he had most definitely seen things. Some of the other photos showed crowds of civilians in Afghanistan, and I wondered if they had ever met this soldier.

This was the beginning of the connections I made between the pieces, and between the history shown within them and the events going on today. For example, a 2006 photograph showed a Palestinian man and his kids in the rubble of their former home. I realized the kids were now adults, and the man was now old. I wondered what lives they had lived since then and if they were still alive. Another striking photograph showed a lone boy on the top of a train, likely aiming to cross the US-Mexico border. I wondered if he had made it, and if he was still here, or deported. It is one thing to hear about death and deportation on the news, but it is another thing to look into the eyes of the people affected by that news.

These people were more than just victims though. I saw an old man in a UN refugee camp. When I looked at him, I saw a strong sense of defiant pride, resonating from every wrinkle on his face. I knew he had lived a life four times as long as mine, and that there was so much more to him than that one emotion, and yet in that image, that pride was all I could see. To me, that is how he would be remembered. Another photo that struck me was a lone man standing in front of several armored cars and armed personnel, protesting the Dakota Access Pipeline which was being built on Reservation land. I wondered how the men thought of themselves, facing a lone man with all that protection. How could they not see themselves as cowards? If you are armed facing the unarmed and courageous, how can you still think you are right? In the picture, it seems obvious, but maybe I'm oversimplifying.

Anyways, I still don't know if there is an indomitable human spirit, but I know that there is a shared human world. These photos aren't isolated—they overlap each other and my own life. Many of the conflicts and situations shown in the photos continue to this day. New photos are being taken, capturing flashes of lives just as rich as mine. However, I will never meet these people, and I will never be able to see their lives, only these brief flashes. If anything, this makes me feel isolated. We're all connected, and yet I'm exposed to a tiny fraction of it all, and I worry about a lot of stupid things that only affect me. Viewing this exhibit motivates me to travel the world and gain new perspectives and hopefully make a tangible difference in the lives of others.

experiences.title: COLOQUIO: Rethinking Human Rights through the African Diaspora
experiences.subtitle: A Brazilian Perspective — Dr. Sant’Ana
experiences.body:
I attended this event because of my history minor. I learned a bit about Brazilian history in my senior year of high school, where my IB history course briefly covered the country's economy and how it changed during WWII. This talk provided the opportunity to learn more about Brazilian history, Brazilian figures, and how it is overall intertwined with the history of Africa.

During the talk, Dr. Sant'Ana discussed the history of slavery in Brazil. I knew slavery was common in Latin America, as it was in North America, especially during the Spanish colonial era. However, I learned that Brazil was actually the last (or maybe one of the last) Latin American countries to eradicate slavery (in 1888). This followed the 1871 Law of the Free Womb, which meant that people born to slaves were considered free. However, Dr. Sant'Ana discussed how this initial step left many still reliant on their would-be masters because they lacked the means to live independently in a system based on slavery. She also discussed the establishment of hidden settlements in remote areas known as quilombos, where anti-slavery thought brewed. Finally, she went over four important thinkers who dismantled the framework of slavery that ran through Brazil, indicating the persistence of a racial caste system far after slavery itself was abolished.

Overall, the activity connected to my wish to understand different cultures and their unique histories. It served to broaden my horizons beyond my geographic and cultural bubble in Florida, and for that, I am grateful.

experiences.title: COLOQUIO: The People in the Kaleidoscope — Bolsonarist Discourse
experiences.subtitle: Contemporary Populist Theories in Brazil — Dr. Luz
experiences.body:
This talk discussed the rise of far-right populism in Brazil, in the context of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Dr. Luz brought up the common traits of populism—a common enemy, pitting the masses against the elites, and positioning oneself as an outsider. Bolsonaro's rise contained all of these features. Despite his history in legislation, he used social media to position himself as an outsider to a Brazilian political institution widely considered corrupt. He pushed the idea that most Brazilians were pious, hardworking people that were being oppressed by an elite political class that only he could combat. With this us vs. them mentality, a clear enemy, an image as an outsider, and a strong command of social media, Bolsonaro won the election in 2018.

I thought the talk was interesting because I definitely see parallels in the US, specifically with the rise of Trump and a lot of the left as well, regarding the populist rhetoric. In the end, I came to see populism as not a good or bad thing, but a tool. In some cases, the tool can be used to manipulate people tired of a corrupt system to accept a system just-as or even more corrupt, but that is not necessarily the case. To speak in generalities, as populists often do, is to lack nuance, glossing over the humanity of the "enemy." Nevertheless, for people who are oppressed, the message of populism is strong and righteous, and who are we to argue that they shouldn't stand up. One must simply be careful who to trust, no matter how compelling their message. Otherwise, we may not know if we are standing up for ourselves, or using our strength to push up another for their own gain.

reflection.title: So What? Now What? — Science With a Human Pulse
reflection.wordCountTarget: 700+ Word Capstone Synthesis (Click Any Paragraph in Edit Mode to Write/Edit)
reflection.leadPullQuote: In front of a waterfall in Iceland, reflecting back on a week of kindness and coffee in Bogotá, I realized I did not want a scientific career detached from the people living on the landscapes I study.

pillars.heading: I. Stepping Outside the Geographic & Disciplinary Bubble
pillars.body: When I began my journey at the University of Florida as a Geology and Microbiology double major, it was easy to treat science as a self-contained puzzle of rocks, water tables, and microbes. Adding a History minor and engaging with the International Scholars Program challenged me to look up from the microscope. Attending colloquia on Afro-Brazilian quilombos and post-1888 abolition, analyzing populist rhetoric in Brazil alongside U.S. political currents, and learning how invasive pines threaten South African water reservoirs taught me that ecological and historical systems are deeply intertwined. Every landscape carries a human memory, and every environmental crisis carries a human cost.

pillars.heading: II. Two Moments of Clarity: Bogotá’s Table & Reykjavík’s Waterfall
pillars.body: The contrast between my week in Bogotá, Colombia, and my research conference in Reykjavík, Iceland, became the defining inflection point of my undergraduate years. In Colombia, Lucia and her family welcomed me—someone they had met for only two days at a music festival—into their home and finca with extraordinary warmth. Over home-cooked rice, Colombian coffee, games of dominoes, rock climbing in Suesca, and candid conversations about Colombia’s civil conflict, I saw how human generosity dissolves cultural guardedness. Weeks later, standing before a waterfall in Iceland after presenting my scientific research, I thought about academia. I loved the rigor of research, yet looking at that waterfall, I realized that even the most profound scientific discoveries would feel hollow to me without a human element.

pillars.heading: III. Now What? Planetary Exploration, Astrobiology & Global Service
pillars.body: As I graduate from UF, the question of 'Now What?' has a clear answer. Just as the photographs in the Harn Museum’s 'One World' exhibit reminded me that we inhabit a single shared human world, my experiences in Colombia and Iceland shaped my commitment to pair frontier astrobiology—at IMPRESS Spaceworks Co. and in my future PhD studying cold-loving microbes in Antarctica—with science communication and international volunteering that connect directly with communities around the globe.
